query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 1–3 at.% aluminum to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in-situ formation of a continuous, adherent alumina scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy with a baseline composition lacking significant amounts of oxide‐forming elements like aluminum.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by incorporating 1–3 at.% aluminum during conventional arc-melting synthesis followed by a homogenization heat treatment.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation at approximately 1200°C in an air atmosphere for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a protective alumina (Al2O3) scale that adheres to the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, as an oxide‑forming element, facilitates the in-situ development of an adherent and continuous Al2O3 layer on the alloy surface, which retards oxygen ingress and minimizes further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-modified alloy will exhibit significantly lower mass gain and more uniform, dense oxide scales compared to the untreated alloy when exposed to 1200°C in air for 100 hours.
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloy samples without the additional 1–3 at.% aluminum, processed under identical synthesis and heat treatment conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be beneficial for refractory high-entropy alloys processed by arc-melting and homogenization under prolonged high-temperature oxidation conditions (≈1200°C in air for 100 hours), while care must be taken to avoid excessive Al that might form brittle intermetallic compounds.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the selected Al concentration provides the optimal balance between oxidation resistance and mechanical property retention; additional concentration gradients may need exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one with the baseline composition and one modified with 1–3 at.% aluminum. Synthesize both sets via conventional arc-melting followed by a homogenization heat treatment. Then, subject both sample sets to isothermal oxidation testing at 1200°C in air for 100 hours. After exposure, perform mass gain measurements, cross-sectional microscopy (SEM) coupled with EDS for scale composition analysis, and evaluate the integrity and adherence of the oxide layers.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (to assess oxidation rate)
Thickness and continuity of the oxide scale (via SEM imaging)
Phase identification of oxides (using XRD or EDS analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass gain and fail to form a uniform, adherent alumina scale compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 []. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [,,,,]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [,,]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [,,,]. Unfortunately, elements Al, Cr, and Si very easily form brittle intermetallic compounds with other refractory elements, resulting in reduced mechanical properties of RHEAs [,,]. A

However, the research on high-temperature oxidation of HEAs is still limited, and many issues in the process of high-temperature oxidation are not very clear due to the complexity of alloy compositions []. On the basis of previous studies, our group proposed a new high-entropy alloy with a new component and performed first-principles calculations [] on its related properties. Subsequently, we carried out research on the high-temperature oxidation properties of this new high-entropy alloy. In this paper, high-temperature oxidation experiments on three kinds of AlTiNiCuCox (x = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) series HEAs were carried out to investigate the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the HEAs under the same temperature. The oxidation kinetics curve was derived from the experimental results. The phase composition, microstructure, and structure of the oxide layer were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive spectrometry (EDS), and the oxidation mechanism was discussed. This paper can provide a reference for the design of new HEAs with high-temperature oxidation resistance.

Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al.
